statement: In Busia’s research-assisted on-farm trials, half-teaspoon CAN top-dressing produced a mean calculated seasonal return of 36%, while the full Ministry-recommended fertilizer/hybrid-seed package had a negative mean return; higher physical yield did not make every input configuration profitable.

sources.supports: Randomised adjacent plots, dose-specific yield and calculated return comparisons.

counterevidence: Small plots, assisted application and noisy seasonal returns; risk and labour assumptions affect interpretation.
inference_limits: Identifies tested plot-package performance under those conditions, not farm-wide realised profits or a profitable dose for every farmer.

test.mechanism_chain: Specified dose/package -> changed input application -> yield less input cost -> calculated return
test.strongest_rival: All fertilizer packages have uniformly high private returns, versus configuration-specific economics.
test.discriminating_observation: Compare net returns, not only yields, across randomised doses/packages.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S02 Table1: positive mean return at half teaspoon; negative at one teaspoon and full official package.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Labour/assistance, small-plot noise and heterogeneous future conditions limit economic transportability.

statement: Randomised harvest-time SAFI offers increased household fertilizer use in treated seasons (adjusted +14.3pp and +18.1pp in the two main seasons), but did not produce a detectable persistent increase after the offer ceased.

sources.supports: Season-specific randomised offer effects and follow-up coefficients.

counterevidence: About one-quarter of originally sampled farmers lacked adoption data; full-control denominators smaller. Persistent effects could be smaller than study precision.
inference_limits: Household any-plot use, not stable individual habit, market-wide diffusion or sustained welfare gain.

test.mechanism_chain: Early delivered purchase offer -> additional acquisition/use this season -> possible learning/wealth change -> later use
test.strongest_rival: One use permanently changes knowledge, wealth or habit enough to maintain increased adoption.
test.discriminating_observation: Positive later-season effects when original offer is absent.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S01 Table4 shows treatment-season gains and later estimates near comparison-group usage.
test.remaining_ambiguity: No detectable persistence does not prove no learning; liquidity, shocks or small scale may offset learned benefits.

statement: SAFI’s pattern is consistent with procrastination/commitment mechanisms, but does not uniquely identify present bias: late free delivery estimated +9–10pp without significance, the early–late difference had p=.08, and timing-choice take-up did not fully match the simple model.

sources.supports: Timing arms, prechoice, maize-purchase test, pilot intention/purchase gaps and alternative explanations.

counterevidence: Seasonal liquidity, opportunity costs, trusted delivery and a surprise late offer can also matter; pilots use purchases rather than subsequent use.
inference_limits: No independently elicited present-bias parameter. Cannot equate one insignificant arm with zero or read welfare rankings directly from trial outcomes.

test.mechanism_chain: Harvest-time small acquisition-cost reduction -> earlier purchase/less delay -> more seasonal use
test.strongest_rival: Time-consistent farmers with seasonal resources, fixed costs and changing opportunities also prefer early offers.
test.discriminating_observation: Announce late offers in advance; vary liquidity independently; directly elicit intertemporal choices and relate them prospectively to response.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S01 includes timing prechoice, favourable maize-purchase test and smaller announced-delay pilots; these constrain some simple rivals, but p=.08 timing contrast and model misfit remain.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Several timing and saving motives share predictions; favourable maize sale is not a complete liquidity intervention.

statement: Among 489 surveyed Indonesian seaweed growers, 86% could not state their current pod size and 87% could not state an optimal size, whereas most could state spacing; these beliefs were elicited before uptake outcomes and alongside observed farm practices.

sources.supports: Input-specific knowledge responses and independently recorded plot practices.

counterevidence: Being unable to answer in grams may partly reflect measurement language rather than complete lack of practical knowledge.
inference_limits: A bounded descriptive contrast, not a universal cognitive deficit among farmers.

test.reason: Reports baseline answers and the measurement design without assigning a psychological cause.

statement: In the seaweed trial, input changes were more evident after personalised summaries than after trial participation alone; measured pod-size phase differences were significant, but the approximately 7g post-summary treatment effect itself was imprecise.

sources.supports: Post-summary self-reported change +0.162/+0.171; pod-size effects 6.951/7.316g; phase-difference p=.003/.015; fixed-effect post-summary p=.14.

counterevidence: Self-reported phase-difference equality not rejected (p=.148/.221); spacing did not change. All treated farmers received summary later, rather than randomising explanation time separately.
inference_limits: Randomised trial-package versus control supports effects of exposure path, not a pure independently randomised summary-only effect or long-run income improvement.

test.mechanism_chain: On-plot trial plus later interpreted results -> information usable for input choice -> subsequent pod-size/practice changes
test.strongest_rival: Experience alone eventually causes learning; later change need not arise specifically from noticing.
test.discriminating_observation: Separate trial-only, delayed-learning and summary-only arms at the same follow-up date, with objective practices.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S03 TableIV provides randomised treated/control contrasts at two stages and objective weights; phase differences for weights support a change after summaries.
test.remaining_ambiguity: No independent summary timing randomisation; direct effect precision is weak and farmer demand effects possible.

statement: Limited attention is a plausible account of the seaweed input-specific pattern, but explanation also reduces computational demands and can alter credibility; the evidence does not isolate attention as the sole mechanism.

sources.supports: Authors consider labour costs, numeracy and perceptibility; farmers knew a summary was coming.

counterevidence: Baseline differences across input dimensions support attention; however, spacing and weight tasks need not impose the same calculation burden.
inference_limits: No laboratory findings borrowed from cited papers; neither an innate deficit nor irrationality established. The model itself allows costly attention to be chosen optimally given mistaken priors.

test.mechanism_chain: Unnoticed input dimension -> raw experience not encoded -> salient explanation -> changed practice
test.strongest_rival: Summary makes arithmetic easier, provides trusted advice or simply arrives after enough time.
test.discriminating_observation: Vary salience while holding calculations, recommendation and timing fixed; independently measure attention/recall.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S03 baseline knowledge plus measurements fits attention; §IV.C explicitly discusses computational rival and footnote29 notes anticipated summaries.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Belief reports are stronger than inference from uptake alone but not direct attention measurement.

statement: In the 120-village Malawi extension experiment, performance incentives to ordinary peer communicators increased their experimentation/communication and downstream adoption; simply appointing local communicators without incentives did not reliably produce that diffusion.

sources.supports: Cross-randomised communicator/incentive design, knowledge exams and observed practices.

counterevidence: Peer strategy used five communicators versus one lead farmer; number, relevance and identity not separately randomised. Incentives can signal priorities as well as pay for effort.
inference_limits: Supports incentive-dependent communication in this institutional programme, not a universal claim that peers need payment or that ordinary identity alone causes adoption.

test.mechanism_chain: Performance reward -> communicator effort/own demonstration -> recipient knowledge -> farm adoption
test.strongest_rival: Passive diffusion follows automatically from selecting respected/local farmers, without effort incentives.
test.discriminating_observation: Cross-randomise rewards; observe communicator actions and recipient knowledge/practices rather than correlate friends’ uptake.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S05 documents weak unincentivised effects and stronger rewarded peer communication/adoption.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Payment, task salience, number of contacts and demonstrator adoption interact; identity-versus-number remains unresolved.

statement: In the separate 200-village Malawi network experiment, central-seed targeting increased pit-planting diffusion relative to extension-worker selection; adoption-rate differences were significant in year two but not year three, and 45% of benchmark villages had no non-seed adopter after three years.

sources.supports: Same two seed slots across four selection arms; diffusion rates and any-non-seed village outcome.

counterevidence: Some benchmark villages did diffuse; most farmers still did not adopt even under central targeting. Network collection expensive; CRM differs from pit planting.
inference_limits: No necessity edge warranted. The larger village-level probability of any adoption and average individual uptake are different estimands.

test.mechanism_chain: Network-based choice of two trained seeds -> wider relevant contacts -> some non-seed adoption
test.strongest_rival: Any two locally selected informed farmers eventually yield equivalent reach over observed time.
test.discriminating_observation: Hold training/seed count fixed and randomise selection rule; compare both average adoption and stalls.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S04 reports ~3pp rate advantage in years2/3, precise only year2, and fewer no-diffusion villages under central targeting.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Three years cannot establish permanent stalls; centrality co-varies with other seed attributes.

statement: Female-reserved communicator roles in the Malawi 143-village study elicited lower recipient ratings and lower training attendance despite comparable measured communicator knowledge/use; pooled downstream knowledge/adoption and yields did not show a precise corresponding gender penalty.

sources.supports: Objective competence, recipient ratings, training attendance, knowledge/adoption/yields measured separately.

counterevidence: Some female-recipient knowledge/adoption contrasts are negative at p<.10; pooled imprecision is not equivalence. Unreserved roles not exclusively male by design.
inference_limits: Identifies effects of reservation arrangements, not a biological sex effect or complete causal mediation through prejudice.

test.mechanism_chain: Reservation changes messenger composition -> recipient appraisal/contact -> possible learning/adoption change
test.strongest_rival: Lower reception simply reflects lower measured technical competence or necessarily creates lower final diffusion.
test.discriminating_observation: Compare objective communicator competence, independent recipient perceptions and downstream results within assignment arms.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S06 finds no measured learning gap, lower attendance/ratings, but weak pooled downstream penalties.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Selected communicators may differ on unmeasured teaching qualities; perception elicitation after assignment and heterogeneous subgroup results limit mediation claims.

statement: The Malawi network data support a multiple-contact learning interpretation, but complex contagion is not uniquely established: connectedness can change exposure, demonstration and persuasion as well as reinforcement of beliefs.

sources.locator: §5 and pp.5–6; individual two-seed link analysis
sources.supports: Two-seed connections predict learning/adoption under randomised seed assignments; author explicitly notes alternatives.

counterevidence: Larger effects where baseline knowledge low and land more suitable are consistent with learning; neither is exclusive to a threshold mechanism.
inference_limits: Do not turn network topology into a universal psychological threshold or infer that one contact never suffices.

test.mechanism_chain: Multiple informed connections -> reinforced useful information -> learning/adoption
test.strongest_rival: More contacts increase encounter probability, effort or demonstrator relevance without a discrete reinforcement threshold.
test.discriminating_observation: Hold contact time/content and seed effort constant while varying independent sources; measure belief updating before use.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S04 uses assignment-induced two-seed exposure and knowledge; PSY-S05 demonstrates that communication effort itself can respond to incentives.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Cross-study comparison suggests a rival rather than jointly identifying a mechanism; studies share institutions and researchers.

statement: In Humes et al.’s 154-completer trial, both effective audiology-fitted and consumer-selected preset aids improved major hearing-benefit measures versus placebo, while satisfaction and preliminary keep intention differed and daily logged use did not differ significantly across service arms.

sources.locator: Results, Figures6–10; Table5; preliminary decision-to-keep section
sources.supports: Randomised service comparisons with several distinct outcomes; 81% versus55% versus36% preliminary keep intention.
CST test was at +1dB SNR, not originally reported +3dB.

counterevidence: Selected volunteers, short period, no prior use and same hardware; absence of significance is not proof identical efficacy. Speech-test calibration corrected.
inference_limits: The intention percentages are not actual final retention rates. Consumer model simulated OTC access within a clinic; does not verify all OTC products or user groups.

test.mechanism_chain: Effective amplification plus specified delivery -> task benefit -> satisfaction/use/retention decisions
test.strongest_rival: Professional contact/placebo alone accounts for apparent hearing gains, or usage alone measures all benefit.
test.discriminating_observation: Same hardware with placebo programming and blinded outcome assessment; separate benefit, hours and choice.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S07 active models beat placebo on benefit, but usage fails to separate groups; S13 corrects test calibration.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Fitting, orientation and interpersonal service bundled; post-trial rescue fitting not independently randomised.

statement: The hearing-aid price comparison was not randomised: earlier participants paid $3,600 and later participants $600; the null price findings for many benefit measures and concentration of returns at the high price cannot identify a causal price effect.

sources.locator: Introduction final paragraphs; Methods Trial Design; final returns section
sources.supports: Sequential cohorts; 17/20 returners paid high price, versus60/134 keepers.

counterevidence: Price cohorts were roughly balanced across service arms, but that does not randomise price or remove recruitment/time confounding.
inference_limits: Neither price irrelevance nor a quantified affordability effect inferred.

test.reason: Methodological fact and observed cohort association; deliberately no causal claim about price.

statement: In Wallhagen’s 91 Bay Area help-seeking dyads, independently elicited accounts linked visible hearing aids with age, disability and perceived competence; some participants rejected or discounted stigma, especially in supportive relationships.

sources.locator: Methods; Results: altered self-perception, ageism/vanity and supportive/nonsupportive others
sources.supports: Separate repeated interviews elicited meanings and reasons before/after choices, including contrary accounts.

counterevidence: Self-reports may rationalise decisions, and stigma can coexist with costs and poor benefit. Participants already seeking assessment; predominantly White.
inference_limits: Evidence establishes heterogeneous expressed meanings, not universal innate preferences, a stigma prevalence estimate or a causal effect of de-stigmatisation.

test.mechanism_chain: Social meanings of visible aids -> anticipated social response/identity cost -> help-seeking or use decision
test.strongest_rival: Low experienced benefit/cost explains refusal, and identity narratives are post-hoc rationalisation.
test.discriminating_observation: Measure concerns before decisions and manipulate social framing/support while holding device benefit/access fixed.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S09 uses repeated separate interviews and follows decisions, including supportive and unconcerned participants; no framing experiment.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Narratives establish a plausible local mechanism but cannot estimate mediation or independently establish actual discrimination.

statement: In a separate earlier Indiana volunteer cohort, 105 of 139 analysed never-users purchased hearing aids and 21 purchasers returned them; returners had poorer measured aided outcomes, while nonpurchasers differed mainly in perceived difficulties and expectations.

sources.locator: Methods Participants; Abstract; Results adherent/nonadherent and keep/return comparisons
sources.supports: Analytic sample and outcome associations after controlling for hearing severity.

counterevidence: Only34 nonpurchasers returned for measurement; only 15 of 21 returners completed end-of-trial outcomes. Unmeasured confounding and selective participation.
inference_limits: These are research-volunteer analytic denominators, not population adoption/abandonment rates. No claim that beliefs cause purchase or poor benefit alone causes return.

test.reason: Original observational associations and counts; separate stages of adoption without a causal preference inference.

statement: For Bihar’s bicycle-grant exposure, the adjusted triple-difference estimate was +5.2pp in age-appropriate grade-9 enrolment/completion for girls, relative to older cohorts, boys and Jharkhand; it is not an estimate of actual cycling or total lifetime secondary enrolment.

sources.supports: Age14–15 versus16–17; female/male; Bihar/Jharkhand; full-controls N=30,112, coefficient0.052(SE0.025).

counterevidence: Estimate falls from0.103 without controls to0.052 with household controls; no randomised rollout. Concurrent state reforms remain a concern.
inference_limits: Causal interpretation conditional on difference-in-differences assumptions and age/cohort comparability.

test.mechanism_chain: Earmarked grant -> more feasible school access -> age-appropriate grade9 participation
test.strongest_rival: General Bihar reform or household/cohort composition would create similar measured change without bicycles.
test.discriminating_observation: Check gender/state/cohort pretrends, socioeconomic controls and ineligible-grade placebo.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S10 Tables1/2/8: triple-difference pretrend not rejected; grade8 placebo near zero; adjustment materially reduces estimate.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Tests cannot exclude all cohort-specific female reforms or ascertain individual bicycle use.

statement: Bihar’s distance heterogeneity and ineligible-grade placebo favour a school-access channel, but do not separate saved travel time, safety, peer travel and changed social norms.

sources.locator: Distance analysis §§II–III; Table8 pp.343–345; discussion pp.346–348
sources.supports: Effects concentrated farther from secondary schools; grade8 placebo0.001; norms/safety discussed as possible channels.

counterevidence: Roads and law/order may complement bicycles even if they do not explain the whole effect; outcomes do not directly measure household norms.
inference_limits: Do not call Bihar a randomised norm-change intervention or treat enrolment as evidence of unrestricted mobility.

test.mechanism_chain: Grant-enabled riding -> lower distance/safety burden -> participation and possible peer/norm feedback
test.strongest_rival: Other reforms or a conditional transfer’s income/incentive effect generate enrolment without norm change.
test.discriminating_observation: Compare distances and noneligible grades; separately measure commute, danger and norms; randomise mobility versus unrestricted cash.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S10 distance gradient and grade8 placebo support access; no direct isolation of safety/norms or cash-only counterfactual.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Several pathways predict the same distance pattern; equilibrium social spillovers not independently identified.

statement: A later Bihar reanalysis finds stronger bicycle-programme estimates in villages with all-weather road connectivity, but its health-facility road proxy and nonrandom infrastructure do not establish that such roads are strictly necessary.

sources.supports: DLHS health-facility access proxy, quadruple-difference estimates and authors’ unobserved-difference caution.

counterevidence: No-road indicator permits dry-season tracks; unobserved village differences and route quality remain. Same main survey/policy lineage as S10.
inference_limits: Contributory infrastructure hypothesis, not independent replication or bounded technical necessity.

test.mechanism_chain: Usable roads plus bicycle access -> reliable travel -> school participation
test.strongest_rival: Road variable proxies wealth, governance, school access or treatment implementation rather than causal complementarity.
test.discriminating_observation: Actual school-route quality and exogenous road changes interacted with bicycle offers.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S12 uses health-facility road connectivity, controls and pretrend checks, finding heterogeneity; cannot observe precise school routes.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Insignificant disconnected estimate cannot distinguish absence from imprecision; no factorial road experiment.

statement: In Zambia’s 100-school experiment, the bicycle-plus-support package reduced self-reported one-way commute by 35.08 minutes (control 103.77) and last-week absence by 0.29 days (control 1.01) at one year; the final article abstract rounds these to 34% and 29%.

sources.supports: 25 payment,20 free,55 control schools; commute N=1,879; absence N=1,952; school-clustered randomisation inference.
Rounded34% commute and29% absenteeism reductions; final full text not acquired.

counterevidence: Differential follow-up and self-report; programme includes mechanics, committees and use restrictions. One-year dropout/grade-transition/English effects not significant.
inference_limits: Effect of the installed package on eligible already-enrolled girls; not a bare-asset effect, school-entry effect or proof all girls can use bicycles.

test.mechanism_chain: Bike/support offer -> usable school transport -> shorter commute -> better attendance
test.strongest_rival: Common schooling improvement explains gains, or mere stated enthusiasm without travel/task change.
test.discriminating_observation: Randomised school control and concrete travel/attendance outcomes, with attrition checks and longer administrative follow-up.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S11 Tables1/4 show large specific effects; S14 abstract confirms rounded direction/magnitude; manuscript attrition bounds inspected.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Self-report not blinded; no independent randomisation of maintenance/custody; follow-up excludes some girls and later records are separately scoped.

statement: Zambia’s nominal-fee versus free bicycle arms did not yield precise differences in first-stage transport or reported empowerment outcomes; a parental-payment/psychological-ownership explanation is therefore not identified by one arm being significant and the other not.

sources.supports: Formal fee/free equality p-values: commute .40; aggregate empowerment .13; agency subscales .11–.99.

counterevidence: Some fee-arm point estimates higher; trial is not a powered equivalence/noninferiority design, and nearly universal uptake limits selection tests.
inference_limits: No general conclusion that charging is harmless, superior or irrelevant for poorer noneligible populations.

test.mechanism_chain: Parental fee -> signal of investment/psychological ownership -> greater agency or sustained use
test.strongest_rival: Free ownership supports agency equally, or physical access dominates; higher fee-arm point estimates are sampling variation.
test.discriminating_observation: Test fee-versus-free contrasts directly and measure ownership/investment beliefs before outcomes.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S11 reports no precise between-arm differences on these outcomes; older abstract’s stronger fee narrative is not adopted.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Only one nominal fee and restricted setting; cannot rule out smaller effects, selective reporting or other fee sizes.

statement: In Zambia’s May2025 manuscript, the package improved selected self-reported agency measures, notably locus of control and bargaining, but general mobility and pooled aspirations were imprecise; aggregate empowerment varies with specification/correction. The final abstract says educational aspirations improved, an unresolved difference from the inspected pooled tables. The inspected evidence does not identify a distinct norm-change mechanism.

sources.supports: Main locus-control0.18SD/bargaining0.21SD; controlled appendix0.16/0.19 with corrected p-values .02/.04 and <=.01. Pooled aspirations0.07(SE0.05) in Table3 and0.06(SE0.05), corrected p=.44/.50 in TableA.11. Behavioural games discontinued.

States that educational aspirations improved; final tables/outcome definitions and pooled-versus-arm-specific interpretation not inspected. This records the version discrepancy, not corroboration of a positive pooled effect.

counterevidence: Aggregate index p-value .04 or .12 across adjustment families in manuscript appendix; no direct normative mediator randomised. Final abstract’s positive aspirations assertion is not reconciled with manuscript pooled estimates; no inference that final tables changed. Asset custody rules constrain movement and resale.
inference_limits: Causal identification is confined to the randomised package’s effects on the measured questionnaire indices in the inspected manuscript. Demand/salience versus deeper agency or norm change is not separated. These are neither unrestricted freedom nor adult earnings/occupation outcomes; final full-text reconciliation remains open.

test.mechanism_chain: Supported school transport -> changed daily constraints/experience -> selected reported agency dimensions
test.strongest_rival: Interview demand, asset salience or family reallocation changes reports without broad social norms changing.
test.discriminating_observation: Independent behavioural or longitudinal agency measures and a design separating response salience/demand from durable control; pre/post questionnaire measurement and multiple-testing corrections alone cannot discriminate this rival.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S11 randomised survey-index contrasts and appendix corrections support some reported dimensions; they do not distinguish the stated response mechanism rival. Behavioural games were discontinued (§4.4.3) and supply no confirmation. S14 aspirations assertion remains unresolved against manuscript pooled tables.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Mechanism among saved time, safety, ownership, school exposure and survey response changes remains underdetermined; self-report not blind.
